stories.headline: Russia Releases Gravely Ill Former US Marine Robert Gilman on Humanitarian Grounds
stories.summary:
Russia has freed Robert Gilman, a former US Marine from Massachusetts who was jailed in 2022 after kicking a police officer while drunk on a train to Moscow. Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev said Gilman was released "for humanitarian reasons" and was aboard a US plane bound for Washington, D.C., on Tuesday. Multiple doctors were attending to him during the flight, and a US official said he appeared to be "in good shape."

Gilman's condition had been dire in the weeks before his release. Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey said Gilman had been "essentially catatonic" and suffering from severe pneumonia, with doctors diagnosing him with dissociative stupor roughly 50 days ago — leaving him non-responsive and unable to eat. His family is awaiting his arrival at a military hospital in Texas.

Gilman's sister credited the Trump administration directly with securing his release. "I am so grateful to President Trump for saving my brother's life," Lexie Hudson said in a statement. "There is no other reason that Robert is alive today other than that President Trump heard about the case and took action." The release comes amid ongoing tensions between Washington and Moscow over the war in Ukraine and the status of other American detainees held in Russia.

stories.headline: Lebanon Votes to Abolish Death Penalty, First Middle Eastern Nation to Do So
stories.summary:
Lebanon's parliament voted Tuesday to abolish capital punishment, positioning the country as the first in the Middle East to formally end the death penalty. A majority of the 128-seat parliament backed the measure, with Hezbollah's parliamentary bloc voting against it. The legislation now moves to the cabinet before going to President Joseph Aoun for his signature; the government has already expressed support.

The vote follows more than two decades of a de facto moratorium on executions — Lebanon's last execution was carried out in January 2004. Courts have continued to hand down death sentences in the interim, and rights groups estimate more than 78 people remain on death row. Under the new law, capital punishment would be replaced with life imprisonment with hard labour, though details on enforcement have yet to be specified.

Civil society groups hailed the vote as the culmination of nearly three decades of campaigning. "We cannot solve a crime with a crime or end violence with violence," said Oragit Younan, co-founder of the Lebanese Association for Civil Rights. The move stands in contrast to regional trends: Jordan resumed executions in June, Israel recently expanded circumstances for capital punishment following the October 2023 Hamas attacks, and the UN human rights chief has expressed alarm over rising executions in Iran.

stories.headline: Solar Eclipse to Darken Parts of Greenland, Iceland and Spain on Wednesday
stories.summary:
A total solar eclipse will sweep across portions of the Northern Hemisphere on Wednesday, with the path of totality stretching roughly 5,157 miles from the Arctic coastline through Greenland, Iceland, and into northern Spain and northeastern Portugal. Totality is expected to begin over the Arctic around 1 p.m. Eastern time, with the eclipse concluding near Spain's Balearic Islands at approximately 2:30 p.m. Eastern. Observers across parts of North America, Europe, and Africa will see a partial eclipse.

The duration of totality will vary by location. Residents of Reykjavik, Iceland, can expect totality to begin around 5:48 p.m. local time and last roughly one minute, while viewers in León, Spain, will experience approximately two minutes of totality beginning around 8:28 p.m. local time. During totality, skies will darken dramatically, temperatures may drop, and the sun's corona will be visible around the silhouetted moon.

Wednesday's eclipse is not the last in the coming years. The next solar eclipse will be an annular eclipse on February 6, 2027, visible across parts of Africa and South America, followed by a total solar eclipse on August 2, 2027, tracking across North Africa — expected to produce the longest period of totality on land since 1991.

stories.headline: NYC Judge Blocks Mamdani's Pied-à-Terre Tax Rollout, Orders Property List Taken Down
stories.summary:
A New York judge on Monday temporarily blocked Mayor Zohran Mamdani's rollout of a new surcharge on luxury second homes valued at more than $5 million, ordering City Hall to remove a supplemental property roll that had exposed the names, addresses, and property values of more than 900,000 New York City homeowners. Judge Wayne Ozzi barred the city from enforcing deadlines against homeowners listed on the roll and prohibited the imposition or collection of the surcharge pending further proceedings.

Attorney Randy Mastro, arguing for the plaintiffs, accused the Mamdani administration of a "botched" rollout, saying the city was required under state tax law to first determine whether properties actually qualified as non-primary residences before initiating the surcharge process. Instead, officials published a sweeping property list and mailed notices that left many homeowners scrambling to prove their primary residences. "The city screwed this up… stop the train and make them do it over," Mastro told the court. He also argued that publishing the property roll had effectively "doxxed" homeowners.

The ruling is a significant early setback for Mayor Mamdani, a democratic socialist who has made taxing the wealthy a central theme of his administration. Supporters of the pied-à-terre tax argue it is a necessary tool to generate revenue from part-time luxury residents who do not contribute to the city's tax base. Critics, including homeowners who filed suit, contend the rollout was legally defective and swept in primary residences that should never have been included in the first place.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Demands Iran Compensate Americans Killed in Attacks as Tehran Seeks War Reparations
stories.summary:
President Trump on Monday escalated the diplomatic standoff with Iran, demanding that Tehran compensate Americans killed or wounded in attacks he attributed to Iranian-backed forces, as well as the families of Iranian protesters killed by the regime over the past 50 years. The demand came directly in response to senior Iranian officials seeking compensation from Washington as a condition for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which Trump called "an interesting idea" before turning it back on Tehran.

In a pair of Truth Social posts, Trump said Iran should pay for deaths linked to roadside bombs, the USS Cole attack, casualties attributed to general Qassem Soleimani's leadership, and the estimated 52,000 protesters killed during the recent five-month conflict. He also called on Iran to compensate the people of Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and Gaza for damages he blamed on Iranian-backed proxy forces. "I have instructed my representatives to put this firmly into any and all future negotiations," he wrote.

The exchange marks a significant new development in the ongoing post-conflict negotiations between Washington and Tehran. Iran has been pressing the U.S. to end its blockade of Iranian ports, lift economic sanctions, release frozen assets, and pay war damages — conditions that have stalled the reopening of Hormuz talks. Trump's counter-demands inject a new and potentially insurmountable complication into those negotiations.

Supporters of Trump's position argue that Iran bears historical responsibility for decades of proxy violence and internal repression, and that any compensation framework must account for American and civilian losses. Critics and some foreign policy analysts contend that demanding reparations from Iran while seeking to reopen trade routes and de-escalate tensions is contradictory and could derail diplomatic progress, leaving the Strait of Hormuz closure — with its significant impact on global oil markets — unresolved.

stories.headline: Syria Sentences Ousted Dictator Bashar al-Assad to Death in Absentia for War Crimes
stories.summary:
A Syrian court on Monday convicted ousted president Bashar al-Assad of war crimes and crimes against humanity, sentencing him to death in absentia in what marks the first formal criminal conviction against him since his regime fell in December 2024. Assad, who fled to Moscow with his family after rebel forces overran Damascus, has been living in Russia since the collapse of his family's five-decade grip on power.

Also sentenced to death were Assad's younger brother Maher al-Assad, who commanded the elite Fourth Division, former defense minister Fahd al-Freij, and four other senior military and security officials — all in absentia. Assad's cousin Atef Najib, the former head of political security in Deraa province, was sentenced to death after appearing in court in a striped prison uniform. He was convicted of crimes including murder, intentional killing of children, and torture leading to death. Deraa is widely regarded as the birthplace of the 2011 uprising, where the detention and alleged torture of teenagers who wrote anti-government graffiti helped ignite the civil war that killed hundreds of thousands.

Syria's interim government has been systematically trying officials associated with the Assad regime since coming to power. The trial was welcomed by victims' families and human rights advocates as a landmark moment, though significant legal and practical challenges remain — most notably securing extraditions from Russia, which has shown no indication it will hand over the Assads or other fugitives.

For survivors and the families of victims, the verdict carries profound symbolic weight. Prosecutor and plaintiff Nouha al-Masri, who lost her brother in the 2011 Deraa crackdown, told the BBC the verdict "reflects the magnitude of the sacrifices we made" but stressed that accountability must continue: "In the new Syria, there will be no impunity from this day forward."

stories.headline: Zelensky Says Russia Fired North Korean Missiles in Zaporizhzhia Strikes Killing Six
stories.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday accused Russia of using North Korean ballistic missiles in overnight strikes on Zaporizhzhia that killed at least six people and injured at least 19. Zelensky said it was the first time Russia "cannot wage war without reinforcements from North Korea," warning that the increasing use of North Korean weapons and soldiers posed a danger beyond Ukraine's borders. He also said as many as 50,000 North Korean troops are being sent to fight alongside Russian forces.

The strikes hit industrial facilities, infrastructure, and non-residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia, according to regional governor Ivan Fedorov, who posted photographs of vehicles and buildings on fire. Separately, strikes on Kyiv damaged a hospital — with staff and patients sheltering — while power outages were reported in Kherson and Kharkiv after substations were hit. Russia fired approximately 120 drones overnight in addition to a range of missiles.

Zelensky also hailed a Ukrainian strike on a Russian petrochemical plant in western Siberia's Tyumen region as a "very significant achievement," calling it part of a broader deep-strike campaign. This came a day after Ukrainian drones killed 13 people in the Tatarstan oil hub of Nizhnekamsk, more than 1,100 kilometers from the Ukrainian border — one of the deadliest single strikes inside Russia since the war began. Ukraine's General Staff said the Tobolsk plant produces rocket fuel components, aviation fuel, and drone materials.

The escalating exchange of deep strikes underscores the intensifying character of the conflict heading into its fifth year, with Ukraine targeting Russian energy and industrial infrastructure to degrade war production capacity, and Russia continuing bombardment of Ukrainian cities and power infrastructure. The Ukrainian Air Force, notably, urged media not to publish "sensationalised headlines" about shortages of air defense interceptors, signaling strain in Ukraine's defensive capabilities.

stories.headline: CISA Holds First Major Election Security Call With State Officials 85 Days Before Midterms
stories.summary:
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency held a roughly one-hour conference call Monday with state election officials to discuss security preparations for the upcoming midterm elections, in what sources described as one of CISA's first broad outreach efforts to states with Election Day just 85 days away. The call was hosted by the National Association of Secretaries of State and led primarily by CISA acting director Nick Andersen, with Jim Harrell, head of integrated operations, also participating.

CISA committed to providing physical and cybersecurity assessments upon request — a standard offering — and recommended election officials work through regional directors, a protocol consistent with past election cycles. Officials on the call acknowledged foreign actors attempting to influence U.S. elections but did not discuss specifics. Known interference attempts by Iran, Russia, and China have been documented in recent election cycles.

Some state election officials expressed relief at the outreach but told PBS NewsHour they have already begun making contingency plans to fill gaps left by CISA's limited engagement to date. Voter registration system security was a notable topic of discussion, an area President Trump has repeatedly raised publicly. Several secretaries of state used the call to press CISA officials on specific concerns.

The timing has drawn scrutiny from election security experts and state officials who argue that with fewer than three months until the midterms, federal coordination on election security should have begun far earlier. The call comes amid broader concerns about the administration's approach to CISA's election security mission, which was scaled back in recent years amid political disputes over the agency's role in combating election-related misinformation.

stories.headline: Update: Ukraine Strikes Russian Oil Hub 750 Miles Inside Country, Killing 13
stories.summary:
Ukraine attacked the petroleum hub of Nizhnekamsk in Russia's Tatarstan region on Monday, killing 13 people and injuring 78 others in one of the deadliest strikes on Russian soil in the four-year war. The Ukrainian military said it hit an oil refinery in the city, which lies approximately 1,200 kilometers (750 miles) east of the Ukrainian border and is home to two refineries and a petrochemical plant. Separately, Ukrainian drones sparked a fire at an industrial facility in the Tyumen region of western Siberia, with Ukraine's General Staff saying its forces damaged part of a petrochemical complex in Tobolsk that produces rocket fuel components and aviation fuel.

The strike represents a significant escalation in Ukraine's long-range drone campaign, which has targeted Russian oil facilities almost daily in recent months. The campaign has caused fuel shortages in Russia, eroded its refining capacity, and unsettled civilian populations far from the front lines. Previous high-casualty strikes on Russian soil were concentrated in the border region of Belgorod; this attack struck hundreds of miles deeper into Russian territory.

In a rare interview with the Associated Press, the commander leading Ukraine's drone war, Robert 'Madyar' Brovdi, said recent strikes in Crimea represent only the first phase of an open-ended campaign aimed at rendering the peninsula unusable as a staging ground for Russian forces. He added that Ukraine could strike seven times more military targets in Crimea if Western allies moved pledged funds more quickly.

The Tatarstan strike marks a new geographic threshold in the conflict, demonstrating Ukraine's ability and willingness to hit deep into Russian industrial heartland. Russian officials have not confirmed what specifically was targeted.

stories.headline: Nvidia and Wall Street Giants Raise $500 Billion to Fund AI Infrastructure Boom
stories.summary:
Nvidia announced Monday it has partnered with some of Wall Street's largest financial institutions — including Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR — to raise $500 billion in capital for artificial intelligence infrastructure. The financing will fund the construction of new data centers, chip manufacturing facilities, and related AI hardware projects both for Nvidia and its partners. The announcement marks the first time major investors are formally treating AI hardware and infrastructure, referred to as 'compute,' as a distinct asset class.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the initiative reflects a structural shift in how AI capacity is financed. 'In AI, compute is revenue,' Huang said. 'We are bringing the world's leading long-term capital providers together to independently underwrite AI infrastructure.' The move comes as the technology and AI industry has collectively spent over $1 trillion in three years on AI projects, driving Nvidia's market value up fivefold in that period.

The scale of the commitment underscores how deeply financial markets have embraced the AI buildout, with companies from Google and Microsoft to OpenAI and Tesla relying on Nvidia's graphics processing units. BlackRock separately entered an individual deal with Meta last month to finance and take a majority ownership stake in a Texas data center.

Some analysts have raised caution about the pace of investment. Jane Sydenham, senior investment manager at Rathbones, told the BBC: 'The worry is that more and more money is going into these projects. Are they all going to earn the right return for the future?' The $500 billion fund nonetheless signals that institutional capital is betting heavily on sustained AI expansion for years to come.

stories.headline: Senate Republicans Rally Behind Thune After Trump Signals He May Back a Challenger
stories.summary:
Senate Republicans are publicly rallying behind Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota after President Trump declined to support Thune serving another term following the 2026 midterm elections. Multiple Republican senators said they would back Thune even if Trump endorsed a challenger, a rare display of distance from the president within the Senate GOP caucus. Trump's displeasure stems primarily from Thune's refusal to abolish the legislative filibuster to advance the president's agenda.

The standoff highlights a recurring tension between Trump's preference for unconstrained legislative power and Senate Republicans who argue the filibuster protects minority rights and long-term institutional stability. Thune's defenders say he has delivered significant legislative wins for the administration while maintaining Senate norms. The dispute sets up a potential leadership fight after the midterms that could reshape the upper chamber's relationship with the White House.

Separately, Republican Senators Rand Paul of Kentucky and Ron Johnson of Wisconsin released text messages sent and received by Dr. Anthony Fauci in 2021, obtained from Fauci's government cellphone, regarding the safety of COVID-19 vaccines for pregnant women. The texts show Fauci discussing how to 'weigh the potential risks against the benefits' of vaccination for pregnant women. The senators are among more than 34,000 messages recovered from the device, according to Johnson's office.

Also in the Senate, Republican senators backed a petition by September 11 families to block New York City mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani from attending the 25th anniversary Ground Zero remembrance ceremony, citing concerns about his past statements. The cluster of developments reflects an active and at times fractious Senate GOP caucus navigating loyalty to Trump alongside independent institutional interests.

stories.headline: Sara Duterte Impeachment Trial Hears Testimony That Confidential Funds Went to Christmas Events
stories.summary:
A state auditor testified Tuesday in the impeachment trial of Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte that her office spent funds designated for surveillance and intelligence operations on Christmas celebrations and tree-planting activities. The testimony adds new detail to a corruption case that has become one of the most significant political proceedings in the Philippines in years.

Duterte, daughter of former President Rodrigo Duterte, faces impeachment charges that include misuse of confidential funds allocated to her office. Critics have argued the funds, which are subject to looser oversight requirements than standard government appropriations, were systematically diverted for non-security purposes. The trial has drawn widespread attention given her prominent political family and her previous standing as a likely future presidential candidate.

The Duterte family remains a powerful force in Philippine politics, and the impeachment proceedings have divided opinion in the country. Supporters of Sara Duterte argue the charges are politically motivated and intended to neutralize a rival ahead of future elections. Prosecutors and government auditors contend the financial irregularities represent a clear breach of public trust and legal accountability.

The outcome of the trial could significantly alter the Philippine political landscape, determining whether Duterte can remain in office and continue as a major political figure in a country where her family name still carries considerable weight.
